The Conclusion says such surface cues support high in-distribution accuracy while hurting transfer.
rubric: Says the paper does not establish in-distribution parity, or says a drop is plausible.
Reason: interp-selection drops the source-heavy surface-cue PCs (PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12) that the paper says support in-distribution accuracy, and no in-distribution numbers are reported.

items.question: Could a reader rebuild the exact full-data Sandbagging greedy set used in Section 4.3 from Appendix D's 'Greedy selection / Sandbagging' row? Use the Jaccard value to explain.
items.answer: Not exactly. The row lists 15 PCs, but Section 4.3 says k = 14. The Jaccard of 0.167 equals 4/24, which fits a 14-PC greedy set sharing four PCs (PC51, PC86, PC62, PC41) with the top-14 target ranking. With all 15 listed PCs it would be 4/25 = 0.16. So one of the listed PCs that is not shared is extra, and the paper does not say which.
rubric: Says the listed row cannot be taken as the exact k = 14 set (it has 15 PCs).
Reason: the Jaccard of 0.167 matches 4 shared PCs out of a 24-PC union (14 + 14), not 15 + 14, so one non-shared listed PC is extra.

items.question: Why might no PC have scored above 6 on the judge's 1–10 OOD scale, given the judge prompt and the judge's own explanations for its top-scored PCs?
items.answer: The prompt is built to be conservative. It asks for the narrowest accurate description, low scores (1–4) for surface, brittle or context-dependent directions, and scores of 5 or more only for plausibly general strategies. Even the general-looking PCs come with caveats in the judge's explanations. PC62 is noisy because honest speakers also deny, PC57 is brittle and lexical, and PC86 gives false positives from politeness or privacy. Those caveats hold the scores down to the low end of the 5+ band.
rubric: Attributes the 6 ceiling to the prompt's conservative scoring instructions (narrowest description, 1–4 for brittle or surface cues, 5+ only for general strategies).
Notes that even the best PCs' explanations list noise or brittleness caveats, which keep their scores moderate.

items.question: PC4 ranks in the top-k target-separability list for all three targets, got the maximum OOD score, and is a top-5 source-probe PC. Why does it appear in none of the full-data greedy sets?
items.answer: Greedy keeps PCs that help transfer when their weights are fit on source data, not PCs that separate the target when weighted on target data. PC4's source-side contrast leans on surface cues such as explicit 'Yes'/'No' turns and defensive phrasing. Its source-fit weight therefore does not carry over well. This is the paper's general finding that the best target-separating PCs are not the ones that keep transferring when weighted using source data.
rubric: States that target separability does not imply transfer once the weights are fit on source data.
Links this to PC4 relying on source surface cues (explicit Yes/No, defensive phrasing), so its source-fit weight does not carry over.

items.question: The top-19-by-variance control contains three Report greedy PCs (PC6, PC9, PC14) and the max-scored PC4, yet it loses badly to interp-selection on Insider Trading Report. Why?
items.answer: PC1–PC19 also include PC7, PC8, PC11 and PC12, along with PC1–PC3 and PC5. These are the PCs the source probe weights most heavily, and the judge describes the first four as surface cues. A probe fit on source data in this subspace leans on them again. The source-PCA probe built on such PCs transfers only about as well as the baseline, so having a few useful PCs present does not rescue transfer.
rubric: Points out that the variance-19 set also contains the source-heavy surface-cue PCs (PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12, and/or PC1–PC5).
Reason: a source-fit probe leans on those PCs, as shown by the source-PCA probe transferring about as well as the baseline, which swamps the useful PCs.

items.question: Why does the Limitations section call the existence of a transferable subspace 'perhaps unsurprising', given the Section 4.1 results?
items.answer: In the same 100-PC space, a target-trained linear probe reaches 0.936, 0.950 and 0.869. So a good linear separator for each target already exists there. Greedy uses target labels to choose which coordinates the source-fit probe may use. In a fully linear pipeline, finding a subset where the source-fit weights roughly line up with that separator is a modest requirement.
rubric: Notes that target-trained linear probes in the same 100-PC space already separate the targets well (0.87–0.95).
Reason: greedy only needs to use target labels to pick coordinates where the source-fit linear weights approximate that separator, which is easy in a linear pipeline.

items.question: Why does greedy selection stop at 8–15 PCs rather than growing toward all 100, even though each added PC gives the probe more information?
items.answer: Each added PC also gives the source-fit probe more room to put weight on directions that do not generalize. The limiting case, training on everything, is the poorly transferring baseline. After the first few transferable PCs, further additions stop raising target AUROC by more than 0.001, so greedy stops.
rubric: States that adding more PCs lets the source-fit probe re-weight toward non-generalizing directions, so target AUROC stops improving.
Supports this with the poor transfer of the full-representation baseline (the 'use everything' limit) together with the 0.001 stopping rule.

items.question: Sandbagging has more evaluation examples than Insider Trading Report (621 vs 255 after removing ambiguous labels). Why does the paper still treat the Report interp result as the more robust one?
items.answer: Robustness here is about effect size, not sample size. On Report, interp-selection gains 0.175 AUROC (0.706 to 0.881) and closes 78% of the gap. On Sandbagging it gains only 0.056 (0.606 to 0.662) and closes 25%. A more precisely measured small effect is still a small effect.
rubric: Says the Report result is more robust because its gain is much larger (about 0.175 vs 0.056, or 78% vs 25% gap closure).
Notes that Sandbagging's larger sample gives a more precise estimate but does not make a small gain larger or more convincing.

items.question: Does PC4 appear in the top-k target-separability ranking (k = 13 / 7 / 14) of at least one target?
items.answer: Yes, in all three. It is 8th for Report, 1st for Confirm and 7th for Sandbagging, all within the respective k.
rubric: Answers yes.
Says it appears for every target, or gives its positions within k (8th, 1st, 7th).

items.question: Does PC4 appear in at least one target's full-data greedy set?
items.answer: No. PC4 is absent from the Report, Confirm and Sandbagging greedy sets, despite its strong target separability and its maximum OOD score.
rubric: Answers no.
Says it is absent from all three greedy sets.

items.question: On Insider Trading Report, do the full-data greedy set and the top-13 target-separability ranking share more than one PC?
items.answer: Yes, four: PC6, PC89, PC14 and PC66. This matches the Jaccard of 0.182 = 4/(13 + 13 − 4).
rubric: Answers yes (four shared PCs).
Supports it by listing the shared PCs or by deriving 4 from the Jaccard of 0.182 with two 13-PC sets.

items.question: On Insider Trading Confirm, do the full-data greedy set and the top-7 target-separability ranking share more than one PC?
items.answer: No, only PC53. This matches the Jaccard of 0.077 = 1/13.
rubric: Answers no (only one shared PC).
Names PC53 or derives one overlap from the Jaccard of 0.077 with two 7-PC sets.

items.question: Does any of PC1–PC5 appear in any target's full-data greedy set?
items.answer: No. None of the five highest-variance PCs is selected by greedy for Report, Confirm or Sandbagging.
rubric: Answers no.
Says none of the three greedy sets contains PC1–PC5.

items.question: Does any of PC6–PC10 appear in any target's full-data greedy set?
items.answer: Yes. PC6 is in the Report greedy set, and PC9 is in both the Report and Sandbagging greedy sets.
rubric: Answers yes.
Names PC6 (Report) and/or PC9 (Report and Sandbagging).

items.question: A team has a modest labeled set from a new target and wants to know, before investing in PC selection, whether selection has room to help. Which of the paper's experiments should they replicate, and how should they read it?
items.answer: They should replicate Section 4.1: train a target-trained probe on the top-100 source PCs with cross-validation, and compare it to the source-trained full-representation baseline. A small gap, as on Confirm (0.874 vs 0.950), means little headroom. Large gaps, as on Report (0.706 vs 0.936) and Sandbagging (0.606 vs 0.869), mean the information is present and the source probe's direction is the problem, which is where selection paid off.
rubric: Recommends comparing a target-trained 100-PC probe (CV) with the source-trained baseline.
Reads the result as follows: a large gap means selection can help (as on Report and Sandbagging), and a small gap means little headroom (as on Confirm).

items.question: A team proposes replacing the logistic-regression probe on full representations with a nonlinear MLP probe trained on Roleplaying, hoping this fixes OOD transfer. Does the paper's evidence support that expectation?
items.answer: No. The paper finds that capacity is not the bottleneck: linear probes trained on target data in the same 100-PC space reach 0.87–0.95. Transfer fails because the source probe learns a direction that does not generalize. A more flexible source-trained probe has, if anything, more freedom to fit source-specific cues. Nonlinear probes are explicitly untested.
rubric: Says the paper does not support expecting a nonlinear probe to fix transfer (untested, or doubtful).
Reason: linear target-trained probes already succeed, so the failure lies in which direction is learned from source data, not in probe capacity.

items.question: A team has labels for only one target and wants to validate an LLM judge the way Section 4.4 does. Can they reproduce that validation, and why?
items.answer: Not as designed. Section 4.4 checks the judge against PCs that appear in more than one target's greedy set, and that requires greedy runs on at least two labeled targets. With one target they can only compare against that target's greedy set. That set mixes in target-specific PCs, so it is a weaker yardstick.
rubric: Says the multi-target validation cannot be reproduced with only one labeled target.
Reason: it needs greedy sets from two or more targets in order to find shared PCs, and a single target's set includes target-specific PCs.

items.question: A team wants a larger interp subspace and proposes keeping every PC the judge scored 5 or 6 instead of only PCs scored 6 in both runs. What does the paper say about how this would perform?
items.answer: The paper does not settle this. Its prompt reserves 5+ for directions plausibly tied to general deception strategies, so 5s are judge-endorsed to some degree. But the paper only evaluates the stricter 6-in-both-runs set. It does show that adding non-selected PCs (the 81-PC ablated set) performs worse, so a looser threshold risks diluting the subspace.
rubric: Says the outcome is untested, or not settled, by the paper.
Notes that only the max-in-both-runs set was evaluated, and/or that adding non-selected PCs (ablated-81) does worse, so dilution is a risk.

items.question: A team with no target labels must choose between a probe on the top-k PCs ranked by source-probe weights and the interp-selected 19-PC probe. Which should they pick, based on the paper?
items.answer: The interp-selected probe. The source-PCA-ranked probe transfers about as well as the full-representation baseline. The interp-selected probe beats the baseline on all three targets, by a lot on Report (0.706 to 0.881). Neither method needs target labels.
rubric: Chooses the interp-selected probe.
Reason: the source-weight ranking only matches the baseline, while interp-selection beats the baseline on every target; both are label-free.

items.question: If PC4 had turned up in all three targets' greedy sets, which of the paper's claims would be weakened?
items.answer: It would weaken the claim that the PCs the source probe relies on are the ones that do not generalize, and the split between source-heavy surface directions and transferable ones (c4, c6). PC4 is one of the source probe's top five PCs, so a source-heavy PC would be transferring on every target.
rubric: Names the claim that source-heavy PCs don't generalize, or the surface-vs-transferable distinction (c4 and/or c6).
Reason: PC4 is a top-5 source-probe PC, so its presence in every greedy set would show a source-heavy direction transferring.

items.question: If Sandbagging's greedy set had shared no PCs with the other two targets' greedy sets, what would happen to Section 4.4's evidence that the judge recovers transferable directions?
items.answer: It would disappear. All five multi-target PCs involve Sandbagging (PC62, PC57 and PC9 shared with Report; PC81 and PC86 shared with Confirm), and Report and Confirm share none. So there would be no multi-target PCs, and the '3 of 5 got the maximum score' check could not be made.
rubric: Says the 3-of-5 multi-target evidence would vanish.
Reason: every multi-target PC involves Sandbagging, and Report and Confirm share no greedy PCs, so there would be zero multi-target PCs.

items.question: Section 4.3 sets k for the probe-weight rankings from a single full-data greedy run (13 / 7 / 14). If the cross-validated greedy subset sizes had varied wildly instead of averaging 15 / 8 / 14, which part of Section 4.3 would be weakened, and why?
items.answer: The fairness of the ranking-versus-greedy comparison, and with it the conclusion that both rankings fail, would be weakened. That comparison relies on full-data greedy giving one stable k that fairly sizes the rankings. If the CV subset sizes had varied wildly, that k would look arbitrary, and the ranking results might reflect a poor choice of k.
rubric: Names the k-matching in Section 4.3 and the conclusion that the probe-weight rankings fail.
Reason: the comparison depends on full-data greedy giving a stable, representative k, which the close CV averages currently support.

items.question: Suppose the source-trained probe on all top-100 PCs (Figure 2, orange) had transferred nearly as well as the target-trained 100-PC probe. Which conclusion from Section 4.1 would fail?
items.answer: The conclusion that the source probe learns a direction within the subspace that does not generalize would fail. Restricting to the top-100 PCs would itself fix transfer, so the case for selecting a subset within the 100 PCs would lose its motivation.
rubric: Names the conclusion that the source probe learns a non-generalizing direction within the subspace (and/or the need for subset selection).
Reason: if the full 100-PC source probe transferred well, projecting onto those PCs would be enough and selection would be unnecessary.

items.question: If the judge had described PC62, PC57 and PC86 as lexical or stylistic surface cues, while they remained in multiple greedy sets, which interpretive claim would lose its support?
items.answer: The claim that transferable directions encode the contrast more abstractly, as deny/deflect or hedging strategies, would lose its support. So would the explanation for why the judge can pick them out. The paper's main evidence for 'abstract' is exactly these judge descriptions of the multi-target PCs.
rubric: Names the claim that transferable PCs encode abstract or general strategies (c6), and/or the judge's mechanism for recovering them (c5).
Reason: that claim rests on the judge's descriptions of these multi-target PCs as general strategies.

items.question: If interp-selection had closed 78% of the gap on Sandbagging but only 25% on Insider Trading Report, which explanation in the Limitations section would be contradicted?
items.answer: The explanation that Sandbagging's modest gain reflects it being the most out-of-distribution target would be contradicted, along with the statement that the Report result is the more robust one. The target described as most shifted would then show the larger recovery.
rubric: Names the distribution-shift explanation for Sandbagging's small gain, and/or the claim that Report's result is more robust.
Reason: the most-OOD target would then show the larger gain, which contradicts that account.

items.question: Does the paper show that PCs which individually separate target classes well do not transfer when fit on source data? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The hypothesis is about PCs that separate the target classes 'by themselves', but the test ranks PCs by standardized coefficients in a joint probe trained on target data. A coefficient reflects a PC's contribution given the other PCs, not its standalone separability. So single-PC separability was never directly tested.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: the ranking uses joint multivariate probe coefficients rather than each PC's individual separability.

items.question: Does the paper show that the judge never gives the maximum OOD score to a PC the source probe weights heavily? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. PC4 is one of the source probe's top five PCs and received the maximum score of 6. The paper notes that 1 of the top 5 source PCs got the maximum score.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites PC4, a top-5 source-probe PC scored 6.

items.question: Does the paper show that targets drawn from the same scenario (Insider Trading Report and Insider Trading Confirm) share a common transferable subspace? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted, at least for the greedy sets. Report's and Confirm's greedy sets share no PCs. Each shares PCs only with Sandbagging: PC62, PC57 and PC9 with Report, and PC81 and PC86 with Confirm.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Reason: the Report and Confirm greedy sets have no PCs in common, and their overlaps are only with Sandbagging.

items.question: Does the paper show that every PC appearing in more than one target's greedy set encodes an abstract, general deception strategy? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted by its own Table 3. PC9 is described as domain-specific lexical cues (medical/leave vs project language), and PC81 as relying on surface and formal cues. Both scored 3 even though each helped two targets.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites PC9 and/or PC81 as multi-target greedy PCs described as surface or domain cues.

items.question: Does the paper show that interp-selection's gain on a target grows with the number of that target's greedy PCs the judge recovers? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled, and the visible evidence points the other way. Among the known max-scored PCs, Sandbagging's greedy set contains three (PC62, PC57, PC86) and Report's only two (PC62, PC57). Yet Report gains far more (78% vs 25% gap closure). The overlap for the other interp-selected PCs is not reported, so no relationship is established.
rubric: Answers not settled (or says the evidence runs against it).
Reason: Sandbagging contains at least as many known max-scored greedy PCs as Report yet gains less, and the full overlaps are not reported.

items.question: Does the paper show that reliance on source-specific surface cues is what causes the full-representation probe's poor transfer? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Only partly. Changing which PCs the probe may use does change transfer: source-heavy PCs give baseline-level transfer, while greedy and interp subsets do better. But the claim that those PCs are 'surface cues' rests on the judge's descriptions, and the authors state these are descriptive, with no causal ablation. So the surface-cue mechanism is not settled.
rubric: Answers not settled (or partially supported).
Reason: the subspace-restriction experiments show which PCs hurt transfer, but the 'surface cue' characterisation is descriptive only, with no causal validation.

items.question: The judge prompt in Appendix B shows each PC's most and least activating Roleplaying examples but not their honest/deceptive labels. What kind of PC could this lead the judge to over-rate, and why?
items.answer: The judge could over-rate a PC whose two poles differ in wording that looks like a deny-versus-admit or hedging contrast but that does not actually separate honest from deceptive responses. For example, both poles might consist mostly of deceptive responses, which is likely because 172 of the 231 non-ambiguous Roleplaying examples are deceptive. The judge never sees labels, so it can only infer deception relevance from the text, not check that the PC tracks the labels.
rubric: Identifies a PC whose poles look like a deception-relevant contrast but do not track the honest/deceptive labels (e.g., both poles mostly deceptive).
Reason: the judge sees no labels, so its score rests only on how the text reads, not on measured label separation.
Optionally notes that the source is skewed toward deceptive examples (172 vs 59 after removing ambiguous ones), so many extremes may share a class.

items.question: Consider a target domain where the deceptive part of each response is a single sentence inside a long, otherwise ordinary assistant reply. Would the paper's pipeline be expected to detect it as well as on the paper's targets, and why?
items.answer: The paper gives no assurance that it would. Activations are averaged over all assistant tokens, so a short deceptive span contributes only a small share of the response vector. Its projection onto any PC, including the transferable ones, would therefore shift only slightly. The pipeline was tested only on the four datasets with this pooling.
rubric: Concludes that performance is not assured or likely degrades.
Reason: mean-pooling over all assistant tokens dilutes a short deceptive segment, so projections onto the PCs shift little.
Notes that the paper only tested its four datasets with this pooling.

items.question: Interp-selection scores each PC on its own, but greedy adds whichever PC most improves AUROC given the PCs already chosen. Why might interp-selection miss PCs that matter for transfer, using the paper's evidence on standalone PC properties?
items.answer: Some PCs may help transfer only in combination with others, because greedy evaluates each candidate conditional on the current subset. The paper shows that standalone properties do not determine transfer contribution. Target-separability rankings overlap greedy sets by less than a fifth (Jaccard 0.182/0.077/0.167), and probes on those PCs can even fall below random on Sandbagging. A per-PC judgment can therefore miss PCs whose value appears only jointly.
rubric: Concludes that interp-selection can miss PCs useful only jointly with others.
Reason: greedy picks PCs conditionally on the current subset, and the paper shows standalone PC properties (target separability) poorly match greedy sets (low Jaccard, target-PCA failure).

items.question: Would the target-PCA probe's good Insider Trading Report result be expected to hold on fresh Report examples that were not used to build its PC ranking, and why?
items.answer: Not necessarily. The ranking comes from a probe trained on Report labels, and the paper describes no held-out split for this ranking. Like greedy, it is a label-informed selection whose AUROC may be optimistic. It is not a label-free OOD estimate like interp-selection's.
rubric: Concludes that the result may not hold, or may be optimistic.
Reason: the PC ranking uses target labels (a probe trained on target data), with no held-out split described, so it is label-informed like greedy rather than a clean OOD estimate.

items.question: Why does the finding that only 1 of the top 5 source-PCA PCs received the maximum OOD score not, by itself, show that the judge scores source-heavy PCs lower than a typical PC?
items.answer: 19 of the 100 PCs received the maximum score in both runs, so a random set of 5 PCs would be expected to contain about one max-scored PC. One out of five (20%) is roughly the chance rate. The more direct evidence that the judge marks source-heavy PCs down is Table 4, where PC7, PC8, PC11 and PC12 get scores of 3–4 with surface-cue explanations.
rubric: States that 1 of 5 is roughly what chance would give.
Reason: 19 of 100 PCs got the max score (about 19%), so the expected count in 5 PCs is about 1.

items.question: Why does Section 4.1 train its target-trained probe in the source top-100 PC basis rather than in a PCA basis computed on the target data?
items.answer: Every selection method in the paper picks PCs from the source top-100 basis. The relevant question is therefore whether that particular subspace contains enough information to separate the target classes. A target-trained probe in that basis reaching 0.936/0.950/0.869 shows that it does, so source-probe failures reflect a poorly chosen direction rather than a missing subspace. A probe in a target-derived basis would not test the subspace the methods actually use.
rubric: Explains that the test checks whether the specific source subspace used by all selection methods contains the target signal.
Reason: success there (0.936/0.950/0.869) shows the failure lies in the direction the source probe learns, not in the basis, which a target-derived basis could not show.

items.question: Using the judge's scores, give a reason why the interp-selected probe on Insider Trading Report (0.881) falls short of the greedy oracle (0.929).
items.answer: The judge's selection differs from greedy's in both directions. PC9, which is in Report's greedy set (and Sandbagging's), received only 3 and was excluded. Meanwhile, PC4, a top source-probe PC that appears in no greedy set, received 6 and was included. Interp-selection thus drops some transferable PCs and admits some that greedy never needed.
rubric: Points to a specific mismatch: a Report greedy PC (PC9) scored 3 and was excluded, and/or a non-greedy, source-heavy PC (PC4) scored 6 and was included.
Reason: interp-selection's subset therefore misses some transferable directions and includes non-transferring ones, unlike the label-guided greedy set.

items.question: If greedy's stopping threshold were lowered from 0.001 to 0.0001 AUROC, would this change which PC greedy adds first for a given target?
items.answer: No. The first step adds whichever single PC most improves target AUROC, which does not depend on the threshold. The threshold only decides when to stop adding PCs.
rubric: Answers no.
Reason: the first pick is the single best PC; the threshold only governs stopping.

items.question: If greedy's stopping threshold were lowered from 0.001 to 0.0001 AUROC, could the selected subsets become larger than 13 / 7 / 14 PCs?
items.answer: Yes. Candidates that improve AUROC by between 0.0001 and 0.001 would no longer trigger a stop. Greedy could therefore keep adding PCs past the current sizes.
rubric: Answers yes.
Reason: small gains that previously ended the search (between 0.0001 and 0.001) would now be accepted, so more PCs could be added.

items.question: If a fourth deception target dataset were added to the evaluation, would the 19 interp-selected PCs have to change?
items.answer: No. Interp-selection uses only the judge's reading of Roleplaying extremes and never looks at any target. The same 19 PCs would be used for the new target.
rubric: Answers no.
Reason: selection depends only on source (Roleplaying) examples and the judge, not on target data.

items.question: If a fourth deception target dataset were added to the evaluation, would greedy selection have to be re-run to obtain a PC subset for it?
items.answer: Yes. Greedy selects PCs by their AUROC on labeled target examples, so each new target needs its own run with labels. The existing greedy sets are also strongly target-specific; for example, Report's and Confirm's share no PCs.
rubric: Answers yes.
Reason: greedy is guided by target-label AUROC and the existing sets differ across targets, so a new target needs its own labeled run.

items.question: Suppose the judge had scored PC62 and PC57 at 3 instead of 6, with about 19 of 100 PCs still getting the maximum score. Would the multi-target greedy PCs then still receive the maximum score clearly more often than chance?
items.answer: No. Only PC86 would remain, so 1 of the 5 multi-target PCs would be max-scored (20%). That is essentially the base rate of about 19 of 100 PCs.
rubric: Answers no.
Reason: 1 of 5 (20%) is about equal to the overall max-score rate of about 19%.

items.question: Suppose the judge had additionally scored PC9 at 6, with about 19 of 100 PCs still getting the maximum score. Would the multi-target greedy PCs then receive the maximum score clearly more often than chance?
items.answer: Yes. 4 of the 5 multi-target PCs (PC62, PC57, PC86, PC9) would be max-scored, or 80%. That is far above the base rate of about 19%.
rubric: Answers yes.
Reason: 4 of 5 (80%) far exceeds the roughly 19% overall rate of max scores.

items.question: A team can only afford a 10-PC probe and wants the 10 most promising PCs from the paper's interp-selection. Can the paper's judge scores tell them which 10 to keep?
items.answer: No. All 19 interp-selected PCs received the same score, the observed maximum of 6, in both runs, so the scores give no ordering among them. The team would need some additional criterion, which the paper does not provide or test.
rubric: Answers no.
Reason: all 19 PCs are tied at the maximum score (6) in both runs, so there is no ranking within the set.

items.question: A team proposes replacing the judge's 1–10 OOD score with a simple yes/no answer on whether a PC is a general deception strategy. Would this discard information that the paper's selection rule actually uses?
items.answer: Largely no. The paper's rule only checks whether a PC reached the observed maximum score (6) in both runs; gradations below that are never used. The selection rule therefore depends only on where the yes/no cutoff falls, which should correspond to the paper's top score level rather than a lower one.
rubric: Concludes that little or no information used by the rule is lost.
Reason: selection only uses whether a PC hit the observed maximum in both runs; lower score gradations are ignored.
Condition: holds if the yes cutoff matches the paper's top score level rather than admitting lower-scored PCs.

items.question: A team reuses the paper's judge prompt but deletes the instruction to give low scores to surface cues, lexical habits and task-specific phrasing. What would the paper's evidence predict about which PCs get selected, and about transfer?
items.answer: Selection would likely get worse. The judge described PC7 and PC8 as deny/deflect-versus-admit contrasts but scored them 3–4 only because they rely on surface cues like an explicit 'No'/'Yes'. Without that instruction they could score as high as PC4 and enter the subspace. These are among the PCs the source probe weights most heavily, and a probe built on such PCs transfers no better than the baseline.
rubric: Predicts that more source-heavy surface-cue PCs (e.g., PC7, PC8) would be selected and transfer would suffer.
Reason: these PCs were marked down specifically for surface reliance despite describing deny/admit contrasts, and source-probe-heavy PCs transfer only about as well as the baseline.

items.question: If a causal ablation of PC62, PC57 and PC86 during inference had shown no effect on the model's deny/deflect or hedging behavior, which claim would lose support and which reported results would still stand?
items.answer: The interpretive claim that these PCs encode general deny/deflect or hedging strategies would lose support. The AUROC results do not depend on the PCs' causal role, so they would still stand. These include the existence of a small transferable subspace and interp-selection's gains over baseline.
rubric: Identifies the interpretive claim about what the transferable PCs encode (c6) as weakened.
States that the transfer/AUROC results (greedy subspace existence, interp-selection gains) are unaffected because they do not rely on a causal role.

items.question: If the judge prompt had also included descriptions of the three target datasets, which property of interp-selection, as the paper presents it, would be compromised?
items.answer: Its status as a method that uses no target data would be compromised. Its AUROCs could then no longer be read as clean out-of-distribution estimates, because target information would enter the PC choice. Without labels it would be less target-informed than greedy, but no longer fully target-blind.
rubric: Identifies the claim that interp-selection uses no target data and gives genuine OOD estimates.
Reason: target information would influence which PCs are selected, making selection partly target-guided.

items.question: The target-PCA ranking uses coefficients from a probe trained on Sandbagging data in the source-PC basis. If the Section 4.1 target-trained 100-PC probe had been near chance on Sandbagging, would the target-PCA probe's below-random transfer still count as evidence against the hypothesis that transferable PCs are the target-separating ones?
items.answer: No. If the target-trained probe could not separate Sandbagging classes, its coefficients would be close to noise, and ranking by them would not identify target-separating PCs at all. The actual 0.869 shows that those coefficients reflect real target separability. Only because of that is the below-random transfer meaningful evidence against the hypothesis.
rubric: Answers no.
Reason: the ranking is only meaningful if the target-trained probe genuinely separates the classes, which the reported 0.869 establishes.

items.question: Does the paper show that its probes detect deception as it actually occurred, independently of how GPT-4o judged each response? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Every honest/deceptive label in all four datasets was assigned by GPT-4o, and ambiguous cases were dropped. The reported AUROCs therefore measure agreement with GPT-4o's judgments, and no independent ground truth is used.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: all labels come from GPT-4o, so the AUROCs measure agreement with its labels rather than verified deception.

items.question: Does the paper show that PC subspace selection improves out-of-distribution transfer for probes of behaviors other than deception (e.g., refusal or harmful intent)? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. All source and target datasets are deception datasets, so the paper tests no other behavior. Its broad framing that OOD robustness is 'largely determined by subspace selection' is evidenced only for deception probes.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: only deception datasets (Roleplaying and three deception targets) are evaluated.

items.question: Does the paper show that selecting a subspace in the source-PCA basis transfers better than selecting a subset of the model's raw activation dimensions? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper motivates the PC basis by not assuming that latent dimensions are privileged, but it never runs a selection over raw dimensions. Its only raw-activation comparison is the full-representation baseline, which uses all dimensions at once.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: there is no raw-dimension subset-selection baseline; the only raw-activation probe uses all dimensions.

items.question: Does the paper show that the target-trained 100-PC probe's AUROCs (0.936 / 0.950 / 0.869) are the best a linear probe could achieve on these targets? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. That probe is restricted to the top-100 source PCs; its purpose is only to show that this subspace holds enough information. The paper reports no target-trained probe on the full representation or on other subspaces, so a higher achievable ceiling is not ruled out.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: the probe is confined to the top-100 source-PC subspace, and no target-trained probe on the full representation is reported.

rejected.question: Does the full-data greedy set for Sandbagging (Appendix D) contain any PC from the source-probe-weight list?
rejected.answer: Yes. PC41 is on the source-probe-weight list (14th) and also in the Sandbagging greedy set.
rubric: Answers yes.
Names PC41 as the shared PC.

rejected.question: Does the Sandbagging top-14 target-separability ranking include any of the five PCs that appear in more than one target's greedy set?
rejected.answer: Yes. It includes PC86 and PC62, both multi-target greedy PCs that the judge gave the maximum score. Even so, the target-PCA probe built on this ranking transfers below random on Sandbagging.
rubric: Answers yes.
Names PC86 and/or PC62.

rejected.question: Does the full-data greedy set for Sandbagging contain any of the source probe's five most heavily weighted PCs (PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12, PC4)?
rejected.answer: No. None of PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12 or PC4 appears in the Sandbagging greedy set. Its only overlap with the source list is the low-ranked PC41.
rubric: Answers no.
Notes that the only overlap with the source list is a low-ranked PC (PC41), not one of the top five.

rejected.question: Does the Insider Trading Report top-13 target-separability ranking include any of the five PCs that appear in more than one target's greedy set?
rejected.answer: No. None of PC62, PC57, PC9, PC81 or PC86 is in Report's top-13. Even so, the target-PCA probe does well on Report.
rubric: Answers no.
Shows that none of the five multi-target PCs (PC62, PC57, PC9, PC81, PC86) is in the list.
